precepts.text: That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love; the will of Christ for the church at Colosse, the same knitting of souls.
precepts.point: Address the perversion head on, as we did last class: souls being knit is not talking about anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church: hearts knit together in love, as joints and bands in one body. Jonathan and David were on one accord; they had the same spirit.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
In 1 Samuel 18, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.” Address the perversion head on: souls being knit is not talking about anything unnatural between the two men.

The same word describes the church. The will of Christ for the church at Colosse was “That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ”. That is the same knitting of souls.

So when Jonathan and David “made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul”, and Jonathan gave David his robe, his garments, “even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle”, it was two brothers on one accord, with the same spirit.

precepts.text: The body, by joints and bands knit together, increaseth with the increase of God; as muscles and joints are knit into one body, so were Jonathan and David of one spirit.
precepts.point: Address the perversion head on, as we did last class: souls being knit is not talking about anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church: hearts knit together in love, as joints and bands in one body. Jonathan and David were on one accord; they had the same spirit.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
The body, “by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.” As muscles and joints are knit into one body, so were Jonathan and David of one spirit.

That is the knitting in 1 Samuel 18: not anything unnatural, but hearts joined like joints and bands in one body, on one accord.

precepts.text: Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell; the same word, the same spirit, kindled against a brother who had done nothing wrong.
precepts.point: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. What was behind that eye? Envy. The envious man is not satisfied with his own portion; Saul had his thousands and still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion, and iniquity dried up his soul from that point forward.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” Wroth is the same word used of Saul: “And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him.” Same word, same spirit, kindled against a brother who had done nothing wrong.

Abel had done nothing to Cain but what the Lord required. David likewise did nothing to Saul but what Saul himself asked of him. Instead of appreciating the song and giving credit where it is due, for the labourer is worthy of his reward, Saul was displeased at his brother's praise: “They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands.” That is the spirit of envy.

precepts.text: Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment, the same judgment as a murderer; anger without a cause is counted as murder in the spirit.
precepts.point: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. What was behind that eye? Envy. The envious man is not satisfied with his own portion; Saul had his thousands and still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion, and iniquity dried up his soul from that point forward.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
Christ took the law, “Thou shalt not kill”, and went into the spirit of it: “whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment.” That is the same judgment as a murderer. Anger without a cause is counted as murder in the spirit.

That is where Saul was. David had caused him nothing, yet Saul “was very wroth”, and the wrath had somewhere to go: “Saul eyed David from that day and forward.”

precepts.text: The envious man hath a wicked eye; that is the eye Saul eyed David with, and the iniquity of the wicked dried up his soul.
precepts.point: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. What was behind that eye? Envy. The envious man is not satisfied with his own portion; Saul had his thousands and still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion, and iniquity dried up his soul from that point forward.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” What was behind that eye? Envy. “The envious man hath a wicked eye; he turneth away his face, and despiseth men.” That is the eye Saul eyed David with.

“A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion.” Saul had his thousands and he still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion: “what can he have more but the kingdom?”

Then: “and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.” From that point forward, that iniquity dried up Saul's soul.

precepts.text: The devils also believe, and tremble; when Saul saw the spirit on David, he who sought David's life became the one afraid.
precepts.point: Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him and was departed from Saul. When Saul saw how quickly David escaped, that spirit on David made the hunter the scared one.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
James says, “the devils also believe, and tremble.” On the morrow “the evil spirit from God came upon Saul”, and this time it came back with more power: “there was a javelin in Saul’s hand. And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice.”

When Saul saw how quickly David escaped, he saw the spirit on David, and he trembled: “Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him, and was departed from Saul.” The one seeking David's life became the one afraid. That spirit on David made the hunter the scared one.

precepts.text: Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company; Saul separated David from his company for no reason, a mark of blessing on David.
precepts.point: But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them; everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man’s sake.”

“Saul removed him from him, and made him his captain over a thousand.” He basically demoted the brother, putting his own armourbearer away from his presence for no reason. Saul separated David from his company, and that is a mark of blessing on David.

precepts.text: In so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head; David's faithful service under a hateful king did exactly that.
precepts.point: But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them; everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.”

David's faithful service under a hateful king did exactly that. “David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the Lord was with him. Wherefore when Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he was afraid of him.” David's continued righteousness heaped coals of fire on Saul. When your righteousness makes the wicked afraid, that is how you know you are in the spirit.

precepts.text: With well doing ye put to silence the ignorance of foolish men; David kept behaving wisely and left Saul nothing to charge him with.
precepts.point: But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them; everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.” David kept behaving wisely and left Saul nothing to charge him with.

And the people saw it: “all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them.” Everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

precepts.text: Godliness is an abomination to a sinner; that is why Saul became David's enemy continually.
precepts.point: The princes of the Philistines went forth, and David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was much set by; harmless as a dove, wise as a serpent.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“The parables of knowledge are in the treasures of wisdom: but godliness is an abomination to a sinner.” That is why “Saul became David’s enemy continually.”

Put the verses together: “Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David”, and he chose to be that man's enemy anyway. If you know the Lord is with somebody and you make yourself their enemy, you have made yourself the adversary.

David was righteous, obedient and humble; Saul was envious, wicked and rebellious, and he could not stand him. As sin is an abomination to the Most High, so godliness is an abomination to a sinner: the sinner cannot bear to look at righteousness.

precepts.text: Cain, who was of that wicked one, slew his brother because his own works were evil and his brother's righteous; the same spirit that was on Saul, the root of bitterness that says, I have to take that man's life.
precepts.point: The princes of the Philistines went forth, and David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was much set by; harmless as a dove, wise as a serpent.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

precepts.why:
“Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”

That is the same spirit that was on Saul, the root of bitterness that says, I have to take that man's life. Saul's works were evil and David's were righteous, and “Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David’s enemy continually.”

Meanwhile David kept on: he “behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul; so that his name was much set by.” Harmless as a dove, wise as a serpent.

precepts.text: Saul took David that day and would let him go no more home; he made David his armourbearer and captain of his host.
precepts.point: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, a young man, and he reigned forty years: seven years over Judah in Hebron, and thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.

note.label: 2 Samuel 5: David Made King Over All Israel

precepts.why:
When the tribes came to Hebron they said, “Also in time past, when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel.” This is where that began: “Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house.”

Saul made David his armourbearer and captain of his host. So even while Saul was king, David was the one leading Israel out to war and bringing them in, and the people remembered it when they came to make him king over all Israel.

precepts.text: David went out whithersoever Saul sent him and behaved himself wisely; Saul set him over the men of war.
precepts.point: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, a young man, and he reigned forty years: seven years over Judah in Hebron, and thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.

note.label: 2 Samuel 5: David Made King Over All Israel

precepts.why:
“And David went out whithersoever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely: and Saul set him over the men of war, and he was accepted in the sight of all the people.”

That is what the tribes meant when they said David was the one “that leddest out and broughtest in Israel.” Saul set him over the men of war, and David fought many wars. The Lord had already said to him, “Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.” He was a captain before he was a king.

So when all the elders came to Hebron and anointed him king over Israel, it was the people who had already accepted him in their sight making it official over the whole nation.

precepts.text: The women sang, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands; David had fame among the people while Saul was king.
precepts.point: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, a young man, and he reigned forty years: seven years over Judah in Hebron, and thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.

note.label: 2 Samuel 5: David Made King Over All Israel

precepts.why:
“And the women answered one another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”

David had fame among the people while Saul was still king. That is why the tribes could say, “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh”: we are kinsmen, related to thee, and we know thee. They remembered the man who led them out and brought them in.

So all the elders came to the king to Hebron, and “they anointed David king over Israel.” He was thirty years old, a young man, and he reigned forty years: seven years and six months over Judah in Hebron, and thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.

precepts.text: Jonathan and David made a covenant because he loved him as his own soul.
precepts.point: That closeness goes back to the beef between Saul and David in the book of Samuel; Jonathan was always there for David, that was David's homeboy, they were really close.

note.label: 2 Samuel 9: David Shows Kindness for Jonathan's Sake

precepts.why:
David asked, “Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” Saul's son Jonathan and David were always very close.

That closeness goes back to the beef between Saul and David in the book of Samuel. Jonathan was always there for David; that was David's homeboy. “Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.”

So even with Saul gone, David remembered the covenant, and sought out whoever was left of Saul's house to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake.

precepts.text: Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David's enemy continually.
precepts.point: The reason for the command is that the enemy may yet repent, as one who persecuted the disciples afterward became one of them.

note.label: Matthew 5: The Sermon on the Mount and the Magnifying of the Law

precepts.why:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you”. The enemy in view here is an enemy within your own people. “And Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David’s enemy continually.”

Saul and David were both Israelites, and Saul was David's enemy continually. That is the kind of enemy Christ is speaking of: your own brother who hates you and despitefully uses you.

Who did this young man learn from? He learned from me. Why should I get mad at this young man? I should be happy. I should walk in here with a smile on my face that this young man who came to me for years was able to break that scripture like that. But that was not Saul.

And in this truth, brothers, the Most High God will always send a brother to help you. In Moses' situation the Most High sent Joshua. And Elijah, the Most High sent Elisha. The Most High will always send somebody to help you. Saul did not recognise that the Most High sent David to make him look good. As a king, what do you need? A strong military. David was a mighty man. Saul did not recognise it. Instead Saul let jealousy and envy overtake him.

note.label: Destructive Behaviors Among Our People

points: And the women answered one another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. At this time who was the king? Saul was the king. David was in the military, David was under Saul. So if I go to war and I am the deacon and you are the captain, and the people say you killed more people than me, why should I get mad? I am over you. So by you looking good, you make me look good. A lot of us do not understand that.

I always said a leader never raises another leader to be like himself. A leader raises other leaders to be greater than himself. The young men you see walking around here, fifteen, sixteen, nineteen, twenty years old, those are the future leaders. As the older brothers, you have to make sure that young man is better than you. How many of you have sons? A lot of you want your son to be better than you. I have heard some of you say, I do not want my kids to struggle like I struggled. So I am going to prepare something, so when I am gone my kids can have that. It should be the same way when it comes to this. That young man that sits next to you, those are your sons. We are the going leaders. They are the coming leaders. Our job is to prepare them for the fight that is coming.

note.label: Destructive Behaviors Among Our People

points: And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him; and he said, They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands: and what can he have more but the kingdom? And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. Do you know that was the farthest thing from David's mind? David loved Saul. David just wanted to be around him. But Saul did not understand that.

note.label: Destructive Behaviors Among Our People

points: And it came to pass on the morrow, that the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house: and David played with his hand, as at other times: and there was a javelin in Saul's hand. And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice. Saul tried to kill him. Just because the people said David killed ten thousand and Saul killed a thousand, when in reality David made Saul look good. But Saul could not accept that. Some of you have that spirit. Me, me, me, why can it not be me? This is not about you. This is bigger than you. This truth is bigger than you. Anybody who walks in here from the street, you are responsible for them. You are sent to wake up the twelve tribes. Do your job.

note.label: Destructive Behaviors Among Our People

points: Saul hath slain his thousands and David his ten thousands. Does it really make a difference if one kills a thousand and the other one kills ten thousand? The enemies are still being put to death. You have two people from the same nation, different tribes, but same nation, same people, same blood, same flesh, walking towards the mark, same goal. You might kill 50, I might kill a hundred; at the end of the day, you're both reaching the same goal.

note.label: The Inevitability of Obsolescence & Agony of Defeat

points: Saul could not understand that David was sent to help him. Brothers can't understand that we are on the same mission towards the kingdom of heaven. One congregation might have more fruits than another congregation; we might be able to reach more masses, but we're still reaching the masses. But with envy and hatred, you can't see that. You become blind and you're moved with lust and power.

They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands. But you only killed a thousand; you want them to lie now. If you only killed 50 people, I'm going to say, oh, you killed 200? No, you only killed 50. They telling the truth. Thou shalt not lie.

note.label: The Inevitability of Obsolescence & Agony of Defeat

points: And Saul eyed David from that day forward: with an evil eye. And Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him. So that envy and hatred came out of fear, because the Lord was with David the same way the Lord is with us if we continue to walk in this blueprint. And the blueprint is what? Just keep the commandments and do the work. Have a zeal for the work. That's it. That's the blueprint.

note.label: The Inevitability of Obsolescence & Agony of Defeat

points: They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands. You the king, but you jealous? Jealousy and envy is a lack of character.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

points: When you don't listen to the Lord, when you try to please other people and not the Lord, you're going to destroy yourself. It is only a matter of time, and it's going to be open to the public; everybody saw the decline of Saul.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

points: Saul eyed David from that day and forward, and cast the javelin to smite David even to the wall. By not obtaining the integrity and not having good moral character, Saul continued to wax worse; his character begins to decline even more over time.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

points: David returned from the slaughter of the Philistines, and the women came out of all cities of Israel, singing and dancing: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Satan was there too, and Satan went to Saul: you hear that?

note.label: Leaven: The Root of Bitterness Part 2

points: And Saul was very wroth. Remember with Cain: why art thou wroth? Did David really slay ten thousands? Yes, he did; the Lord was fighting with David, and David was another level of warrior.

They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands: and what can he have more but the kingdom? He wants my position. That is Satan whispering them things in his mind: the people love David; they are saying he is better than you; watch him. And Saul listened.

note.label: Leaven: The Root of Bitterness Part 2

points: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward: he envied David and became bitter toward him, watching him sideways. Why did that happen? Because Saul entertained Satan. Them thoughts came to Saul's head, and instead of saying, David is a godly man, he does not want my position, he fed into it. The spirit of envy came on him.

note.label: Leaven: The Root of Bitterness Part 2

points: Address the perversion head on, as we did last class: souls being knit is not talking about anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church: hearts knit together in love, as joints and bands in one body. Jonathan and David were on one accord; they had the same spirit.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul, and they made a covenant; Jonathan stripped himself of his robe and gave it to David, with his garments, his sword, his bow, and his girdle.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David went whithersoever Saul sent him and behaved himself wisely, and Saul set him over the men of war, and he was accepted in the sight of all the people and of Saul's servants.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: When they returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all cities of Israel singing and dancing to meet king Saul, with tabrets, with joy, and with instruments of musick.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: The women answered one another as they played: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. The first line honored Saul, but the song made David exponentially the greater warrior, and brothers catch spirits behind what women say and do.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Saul was very wroth and the saying displeased him: they have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands; and what can he have more but the kingdom? Wroth is the same word used in Genesis 4 of how Cain fell toward Abel, and Abel had done nothing to him but what the Lord required; David likewise did nothing to Saul but what Saul himself asked of him.
Instead of appreciating the song, give credit where it is due, for the labourer is worthy of his reward, Saul was displeased at his brother's praise; that is the same spirit of envy.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. What was behind that eye? Envy. The envious man is not satisfied with his own portion; Saul had his thousands and still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion, and iniquity dried up his soul from that point forward.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: On the morrow the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and this time it came back with more power: there was a javelin in Saul's hand, and he cast it, saying, I will smite David even to the wall with it. David avoided out of his presence twice.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him and was departed from Saul. When Saul saw how quickly David escaped, that spirit on David made the hunter the scared one.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Saul removed David from him and made him captain over a thousand; he basically demoted the brother, putting his own armourbearer away from his presence for no reason.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David behaved himself wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him, and when Saul saw it he was the more afraid. David's continued righteousness heaped coals of fire on Saul; when your righteousness makes the wicked afraid, that is how you know you are in the spirit.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them; everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Saul offered his elder daughter Merab to wife, only be thou valiant for me and fight the Lord's battles; for Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him. Remember, the king's daughter was already the promise attached to killing Goliath; Saul aged him out of that and reattached conditions, thinking the Philistines would finish David.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David answered humbly: who am I, and what is my life, or my father's family in Israel, that I should be son in law to the king?

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: When the time came that Merab should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite; Saul tricked David out of her.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David, and the thing pleased Saul: I will give him her, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him. He set his own daughter as a trap.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David again answered humbly, that he was a poor man and lightly esteemed; so Saul waived the dowry money and named his price: an hundred foreskins of the Philistines, thinking to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines, for there was no way he should survive that errand.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David arose with his men, slew two hundred Philistines, and brought their foreskins in full tale to the king; he doubled the order. That is how devoted a warrior he was for his king and his nation, and Saul gave him Michal his daughter to wife.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: David was righteous, obedient, and humble; Saul was envious, wicked, and rebellious, and he could not stand him. As sin is an abomination to the Most High, so godliness is an abomination to a sinner; the sinner cannot bear to look at righteousness.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David, and that Michal loved him, and Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David's enemy continually. Put the verses together: he knew the Lord was with the man, and he chose to be that man's enemy anyway. If you know the Lord is with somebody and you make yourself their enemy, you have made yourself the adversary.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul

points: The princes of the Philistines went forth, and David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was much set by; harmless as a dove, wise as a serpent.

note.label: 1 Samuel 18: The Envious Eye of Saul
